beats.say: When germs get in, your brain cranks up the heat.
beats.cap: WHEN GERMS GET IN, | YOUR BRAIN | *CRANKS UP THE HEAT.*

beats.say: Your body's thermostat sits in your brain, in the hypothalamus.
beats.cap: YOUR BODY'S *THERMOSTAT* | SITS IN YOUR BRAIN, | IN THE *HYPOTHALAMUS.*

beats.say: Germs make your white blood cells release chemicals called pyrogens.
beats.cap: GERMS MAKE YOUR | WHITE BLOOD CELLS | RELEASE CHEMICALS | CALLED *PYROGENS.*

beats.say: So you shiver to make heat,
and blood moves away from your skin to keep it in.
beats.cap: AND BLOOD MOVES | AWAY FROM YOUR SKIN | TO *KEEP IT IN.*

beats.say: A fever usually means thirty eight degrees Celsius or more.
beats.cap: A FEVER USUALLY MEANS | *38°C* OR MORE.

beats.say: The heat makes it harder for many germs to grow,
beats.cap: THE HEAT MAKES IT | *HARDER* FOR MANY GERMS | TO GROW,

beats.say: and helps switch on your immune defenses.
beats.cap: AND HELPS SWITCH ON | YOUR *IMMUNE DEFENSES.*

beats.say: See a doctor if it goes above thirty nine point four,
beats.cap: SEE A DOCTOR | IF IT GOES | ABOVE *39.4°C,*

beats.say: or comes with a stiff neck or confusion.
beats.cap: OR COMES WITH | A *STIFF NECK* | OR *CONFUSION.*

beats.say: So that fever isn't your body breaking.
beats.cap: SO THAT FEVER | ISN'T YOUR BODY | *BREAKING.*

beats.say: It's your body turning up the heat on the germs.
beats.cap: IT'S YOUR BODY | TURNING UP THE HEAT | *ON THE GERMS.*

sources.fact: MSD Manual Professional: the body's thermostat (in the hypothalamus) resets at a higher temperature; fever results when something raises the hypothalamic set point; exogenous pyrogens induce release of endogenous pyrogens (IL-1, TNF-alpha, IL-6); vasoconstriction shunts blood from the periphery to decrease heat loss and shivering increases heat production; fever stimulates immunologic mechanisms and inhibits the growth of some microorganisms

MSD Manual Consumer: fever occurs when the body's thermostat resets at a higher temperature, primarily in response to infection; pyrogens are usually produced by white blood cells (monocytes and macrophages); fever can make it more difficult for microorganisms to grow; 100.4 F (38 C) at any time after early morning is elevated

Cleveland Clinic: providers most often say a fever is 100.4 F (38 C); adult fevers under 103 F (39.4 C) typically aren't dangerous, above that call your provider; an infection fever should pass within three to four days, call if it lingers; go to the ER with fever plus stiff neck, confusion, severe headache
NHS: a high temperature is usually considered to be 38C or above; it's often caused by your body fighting an infection
Cleveland Clinic, Chills: chills are your body's way of raising its core temperature; shivering muscles contract and relax, which warms the body

math.note: NHS and Cleveland Clinic: fever usually 38 C (100.4 F) or above
Cleveland Clinic: above 103 F (39.4 C) call your provider
Cleveland Clinic: infection fever should pass within three to four days; call if it lingers longer

post.instagram_caption:
Your brain gives you a fever on purpose 🌡️

When germs get in, white blood cells release chemicals called pyrogens, and the thermostat in your hypothalamus resets higher. Normal suddenly feels cold, so you shiver to make heat and blood moves away from your skin to keep it in. The extra heat makes it harder for many germs to grow and helps your immune defenses.

See a doctor if it goes above 39.4°C (103°F), lasts more than 3 days, or comes with a stiff neck or confusion.

Sources: MSD Manual, Cleveland Clinic, NHS.
